Abstract:
<jats:p>This study examined the integration of Manufacturing Execution Systems, SAP enterprise applications, and PI Historian platforms for real-time industrial asset performance management. A multisite, retrospective longitudinal, quasi-experimental quantitative design was employed across 18 asset-intensive industrial facilities. The study covered 48 consecutive months, comprising 24 preintegration and 24 postintegration months. Propensity-score matching produced 600 comparable assets, divided equally between high-integration and partial- or fragmented-integration conditions. The final dataset contained 28,224 asset-month observations, 4,286 verified failures, 52,614 condition alerts, 8,932 maintenance notifications, and 8,147 work orders. Data were analyzed using mixed-effects regression, negative-binomial modeling, difference-in-differences estimation, interrupted time-series analysis, survival analysis, recurrent-event modeling, mediation, moderation, and sensitivity testing. High-integration facilities achieved 92.4% interface automation, 99.3% transaction success, 98.7% asset-mapping accuracy, 98.8% data completeness, and 94.1% event traceability. After adjustment for asset, operational, maintenance, facility, and baseline characteristics, high-integration assets recorded a 32% lower failure rate, IRR = 0.68, 95% CI [0.61, 0.75], p < .001, and 51% lower repeated-failure odds, OR = 0.49, 95% CI [0.39, 0.62], p < .001. Mean time between failures increased by 2,310 hours, while mean time to repair declined by 3.08 hours. Availability increased by 2.18 percentage points, overall equipment effectiveness increased by 4.96 percentage points, and annual unplanned downtime declined by 55.1 hours per asset. Throughput attainment increased by 5.04 percentage points, quality yield increased by 1.36 percentage points, annual maintenance cost decreased by USD 12,600 per asset, and annual production-loss value declined by USD 45,800 per asset. High-integration assets experienced a 44% lower failure hazard and achieved a median failure-free duration of 8,420 hours. Real-time information visibility and maintenance responsiveness mediated 53.4% of the integration–performance relationship. The findings established that coordinated MES–SAP–PI Historian integration was associated with improved reliability, maintainability, availability, production continuity, quality performance, and economic control.</jats:p>

A multisite, retrospective longitudinal, quasi-experimental quantitative design was employed across 20 facilities. The observation period covered 48 consecutive months, comprising 24 premodernization and 24 postmodernization months. The final dataset contained 24,470 equipment-month observations, 18.7 million material movements, 1.28 million production and fulfillment orders, 5,248 verified faults, 2,106 safety interruptions, and 3,684 manual recovery events. High-maturity equipment achieved an average controller scan time of 7.4 milliseconds, 99.5% sequence accuracy, 94.8% diagnostic coverage, 87.2% automatic recovery success, and 95.4% supervisory-system integration. Throughput increased by 148 handled units per hour, capacity attainment increased by 7.10 percentage points, movement cycle time decreased by 2.88 minutes, and on-time order completion increased by 5.76 percentage points. Mean time between failures increased by 2,340 hours, mean time to repair decreased by 2.38 hours, availability increased by 2.68 percentage points, and annual downtime decreased by 45.2 hours per asset. Abstract:
<jats:p>The reliability of Internet of Things systems is critical for industrial applications; however, operational reliability data are often heterogeneous and strongly right-skewed, exhibiting non-Gaussian behaviour, overdispersion, and production-level variability that challenge classical predictive maintenance models. Existing approaches frequently rely on pooled assumptions or simplified error structures, limiting their ability to identify latent batch-level degradation and to jointly interpret discrete failure events and continuous lifetime information. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hierarchical Bayesian framework based on Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) to jointly model discrete reset counts and continuous failure times. Three Latent Gaussian Models are evaluated—ranging from pooled baseline specifications to a fully joint model with shared latent batch effects—using a synthetic dataset designed to mimic realistic industrial fault patterns. The analysis demonstrates that standard pooled models fail to capture the degradation dynamics of defective device batches. In contrast, the hierarchical joint model successfully recovers latent quality variations, accurately links high reset intensity with shortened lifetimes, and substantially improves model fit, achieving a DIC reduction of over 67% compared to baseline approaches. INLA provides a computationally efficient and rigorously calibrated alternative to MCMC-based methods for modelling skewed and heterogeneous reliability data. The proposed framework enables reliable identification of defective production batches and robust uncertainty quantification, offering a practical tool for data-driven predictive maintenance in Industry 4.0. Future work will focus on validating the proposed framework using real industrial IoT datasets.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The successful deployment of drones in construction increasingly depends on human operators' willingness to work collaboratively with robotic systems. However, limited understanding of how trust develops during human–drone interaction and its relationship to performance outcomes hampers the design of effective human–drone interaction frameworks and adoption strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a within-subjects experiment with 41 participants who completed collaborative drone flight operations in a virtual reality environment. Trust was measured pre- and post-interaction across four dimensions: perceived risk, benevolence, competence and reciprocity. Objective performance was quantified via task completion time and collision count.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>One-sample t-tests revealed significant increases in trust for benevolence (d = 0.35), competence (d = 0.44) and reciprocity (d = 0.43), with overall trust improving substantially (d = 0.48, p = 0.004). Larger increases in trust were associated with operational performance, inversely correlating with both completion time (r = −0.60, p &lt; 0.001) and collisions (r = −0.71, p &lt; 0.001). Among trust dimensions, perceived reciprocity was the most associated with objective performance in this task, showing significant correlations with reduced collisions (r = −0.32, p = 0.041).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

Abstract:
Consider a mobile robot exploring an office building with the aim of observing as much human activity as possible over several days. It must learn where and when people are to be found, count the observed activities, and revisit popular places at the right time. In this paper we present a series of Bayesian estimators for the levels of human activity that improve on simple counting. We then show how these estimators can be used to drive efficient exploration for human activities. The estimators arise from modelling the human activity counts as a partially observable Poisson process (POPP). This paper presents novel extensions to POPP for the following cases: (i) the robot’s sensors are correlated, (ii) the robot’s sensor model, itself built from data, is also unreliable, (iii) both are combined. It also combines the resulting Bayesian estimators with a simple, but effective solution to the exploration-exploitation trade-off faced by the robot in a real deployment. A series of 15 day robot deployments show how our approach boosts the number of human activities observed by 70% relative to a baseline and produces more accurate estimates of the level of human activity in each place and time.

Zhe-Yuan Hu, Robyn Wu, Naveen Enock, Jasmine Li, Riya Kadakia, Zackory Erickson, and Aviral Kumar. Rac: robot learning for long-horizon tasks by scaling recovery and correction. IEEE Transactions on Robotics, 42:2843-2860, Sep 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2509.07953, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2509.07953. This article has 68 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

RaC (Recovery and Correction) is an iterative imitation-learning data-collection strategy that combines human-provided recovery segments with corrective segments and full expert demonstrations. Recovery segments start from failures or out-of-distribution states and return the robot to familiar, in-distribution states encountered earlier in demonstrations; corrective segments directly advance or complete the current subtask. The central idea is that recovery is often easier to learn than precise task completion, allowing the robot to reset, retry, and reduce the effects of compounding errors. The protocol begins with an initial round of full demonstrations, trains a policy, then repeatedly collects human interventions during rollouts of the current policy, adds the intervention data to the dataset, and retrains. The robot platform uses two 7-degree-of-freedom xArm-7 manipulators with scaled-down soft grippers, supported by overhead and wrist RGB cameras and 60-Hz reactive control. This excerpt does not report numerical intervention rates or task success rates; those figures would need to be obtained from other sections of the paper. It does establish that RaC is intended to improve the scaling slope of task success versus data size by explicitly increasing recovery and correction data.

RaC (Recovery and Correction) is presented as a data-collection framework for scaling imitation learning on long-horizon manipulation tasks. Rather than treating human intervention only as an optimal correction to be copied, RaC deliberately collects recovery segments, correction behaviors, and full demonstrations, treating recovery as a learnable skill. The intervention segment is used to expose the policy to out-of-distribution states caused by compounding errors; under the stated termination rule, the episode ends immediately after the intervention, preventing later subtasks from being recorded under a mixed learned-policy/human state distribution. The method leaves the underlying imitation-learning objective unchanged, attributing gains to improved trajectory/data composition. The excerpt reports experiments on three real-world bimanual tasks—shirt hanging, airtight-lid sealing, and clamshell takeout-box packing—and says RaC achieves higher success rates, steeper scaling trends, and up to one order of magnitude better data efficiency than batched full demonstrations and HG-DAgger-style collection. It also reports test-time scaling: executing more recovery maneuvers can improve overall success by allowing multiple attempts. RaC (Recovery and Correction) is a post-imitation-learning training phase that uses human-in-the-loop interventions to teach policies how to recover from impending failures, retry, adapt, and complete the current sub-task. During a rollout, an operator takes over, rewinds or repositions the robot to a familiar in-distribution state, and then supplies a corrective segment. The excerpt describes Genie Centurion (GCENT) as a real-robot training and supervision framework designed to improve data yield relative to human effort. Its Task Sentinel is a multimodal model that monitors image observations and task instructions, detects whether an atomic step has been completed, and automatically advances when successful. If a step remains incomplete beyond a predefined timeout, it places the robot in “Awaiting Intervention” and requests human help. In Human-Gated mode, the operator intervenes when errors occur; as policy performance improves, Sentinel allows one operator to supervise multiple robots and request assistance only when necessary. When intervention is needed, the operator can rewind up to three seconds using the robot’s state buffer, apply physical corrections, and provide a targeted demonstration. The policy is trained only on these human intervention segments, concentrating supervision on corrective, high-value data rather than complete passive trajectories. Across four real-world tasks—sandwich assembly, connector insertion, microwave heating, and typing—GCENT achieved an average final score of 0.93, compared with 0.38 for passive collection and 0.53 for adversarial collection under the reported evaluation. The paper reports a 55% improvement over passive methods and 40% over ADC with equal data budgets, with all tasks exceeding 0.9 within 3–5 GCENT rounds. {"answer": "
# Human Intervention Metrics, Interactive Learning, Remote Supervision, and Statistical Design for a Laboratory Robot Reliability Campaign

## (1) Intervention Definitions and Reporting Outside Chemistry

### Autonomous-Driving Disengagements

The most mature reporting framework for human interventions is the California DMV's Autonomous Vehicle Tester Program. Under California Code of Regulations §227.38, a disengagement is defined as "deactivation of autonomous mode after an autonomous-technology failure is detected or when safe operation requires the test driver to take immediate manual control" (pqac-00000002). Manufacturers must file monthly disengagement reports (form OL 311R) by the tenth day of each month, recording VIN, software version, GPS coordinates, initiator, cause categories, and post-event actions; separate collision reports (form OL 316) are required within ten days, and hard-braking events above 0.5 g are reported monthly (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005). 

Disengagements are classified by initiator—system-initiated (automated), driver-initiated (manual), or planned for testing—and by cause categories including perception/localization/planning errors, environmental factors, and interactions with other road users (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). The primary performance metric is the disengagement-to-mileage ratio (disengagements per mile or its reciprocal, miles between interventions), though the DMV does not prescribe a standard calculation formula (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Banerjee et al. (2018) analyzed 1,116,605 autonomous miles, 5,328 disengagements, and 42 accidents from 144 vehicles across 12 manufacturers (pqac-00000001). Paz et al. (2020) emphasized that raw disengagement counts are insufficient without normalization by distance, operating time, testing location, and number of vehicles (pqac-00000000). Skokan and Mareček (2025) warned that "manufacturers' reporting thresholds and safety drivers' intervention decisions vary substantially," so reported rates reflect "technical performance, operating conditions, reporting practices, and individual driver risk tolerance" rather than a fully standardized safety measure (pqac-00000006).

### Fleet Learning: Return on Human Effort (ROHE)

For robot fleets, Hoque et al. (2022) formalized Interactive Fleet Learning (IFL) and introduced ROHE as "the expected cumulative fleet reward divided by total human assistance time, with normalization by the numbers of robots and supervisors and an added one in the denominator for the zero-assistance case" (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011). Fleet-DAgger evaluated allocation with 100 simulated robots and a physical experiment with four ABB YuMi arms and two remote human supervisors, achieving up to 8.8× higher ROHE than baselines (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000052).

### Transferability to a Laboratory Arm

Several of these definitions transfer directly:

- **Disengagement-style counting**: Any moment a remote operator takes control or the system is paused maps to an AV disengagement. The LabRobFail taxonomy (preprint, Wang et al. 2026) provides a lab-specific coding scheme with five major categories—Perception Failure (PF), Grasping Failure (GF), Motion Failure (MF), Logic Failure (LF), and Safety Failure (SF)—and 11 fine-grained failure types, plus four severity levels L1–L4 (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037).
- **Operations between interventions** (analogous to miles between disengagements) is the natural lab-arm metric: mean interventions between failures (MIBF) or its reciprocal.
- **ROHE** can be adapted: cumulative successful transfers divided by total human-supervision time.
- **Intervention sample ratio**: Sirius defined this as "the fraction of timesteps completed by humans relative to total trajectory timesteps," reporting a mean of 0.32 with SD 0.11 (pqac-00000020).

**No published standard or reporting checklist** exists specifically for laboratory robot arms. The LabRobFail benchmark is the closest laboratory-specific framework but is simulation-based and was published as a preprint (pqac-00000032).

## (2) Human-in-the-Loop Learning on Real Robots

The following table summarizes the major systems and their reported metrics:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### Key Results by System

**HG-DAgger** (Kelly et al. 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8793698) introduced human-gated interactive imitation learning where "the human expert determines when to intervene and take control of the robot." When reimplemented as a baseline in HIL-SERL, HG-DAgger averaged only 49.7% success with no consistent decline in intervention rate (pqac-00000025).

**Sirius** (Liu et al. 2024, DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273901) introduced intervention-weighted behavioral cloning on a Franka Emika Panda. The weighting scheme "up-weights interventions and down-weights pre-interventions" using approximated human trust (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019). Across deployment data, the mean intervention sample ratio was 0.32 (SD 0.11), with an average of 2.80 interventions per trajectory and 15.28 timesteps per intervention (pqac-00000020). Policy success rates ranged from 44.8% to 72.7% across individual operators, with an overall 27% improvement over baselines on real hardware (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017).

**HIL-SERL** (Luo et al. 2025, DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.ads5033, *Science Robotics*) achieved 100% success on all 13 evaluated tasks within 1–2.5 hours of real-world training, with the intervention rate declining to 0% as policies converged, while HG-DAgger baselines averaged 49.7% success (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029). Training began with approximately 20–30 human demonstrations (pqac-00000027). In a separate evaluation (Lin et al. 2026), HIL-SERL showed human intervention rates of 39–77% across five manipulation tasks before convergence (pqac-00000031).

**RaC** (Hu et al. 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2509.07953, *IEEE Transactions on Robotics*) uses two xArm-7 manipulators and explicitly teaches recovery-then-correction behavior. It achieved 78.3% full-task success on shirt hanging with approximately 5 hours of data versus 75% for ALOHA Unleashed with approximately 89 hours (pqac-00000049). In a head-to-head comparison, RaC achieved 61/100 successful trials versus 22/100 for HG-DAgger (pqac-00000051). Recovery-to-correction frame ratios were maintained at approximately 1:1 to 1:2, and total intervention frames decreased across rounds (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051).

### Low-Cost Arms

**No published HIL/interactive-learning work was found on SO-100, SO-101, Koch, or PiPER arms.** The closest low-cost platform is the xArm-7 used in RaC (pqac-00000046). The ALOHA system uses ViperX arms for bimanual teleoperation but its published work focuses on demonstration collection rather than online interactive learning with intervention-rate tracking. This represents a significant gap: all published HIL-RL and interactive IL systems with reported intervention metrics have used research-grade arms (Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, UR5, xArm-7).

### Laboratory or SDL Tasks

**No published evidence was found** of HIL interactive learning applied to self-driving laboratory tasks or chemical/materials manipulation. This is an open area.

## (3) Remote Supervision and Shared Autonomy

### One-to-Many Supervision

Fleet-DAgger formalized the problem of allocating M remote supervisors to N >> M robots, with physical experiments involving four ABB YuMi arms and two remote humans teleoperating over the Internet (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054). Hoque's dissertation describes remote fleet supervision using a cloud robotics platform supporting "real-time operation with robots, compute nodes, and teleoperators distributed globally" and reports a 10 Hz control loop over the Internet (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055). However, Fleet-DAgger's formal model "assumes that supervisors have perfect situational awareness, can switch between robots without any switching latency, and operate in synchronous timesteps without network latency or communication issues" and identifies removing these assumptions as future work (pqac-00000059).

Genie Centurion (GCENT, preprint, Wang et al. 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2505.18793) demonstrated one-human-to-two-robot supervision in a sandwich-assembly task. As model success rose from 40% to 80%, the intervention rate fell from 47% to 27%, while normalized collection efficiency rose from 1.86 to 1.92 (pqac-00000061). GCENT's Task Sentinel autonomously detects incomplete steps and "requests human intervention when needed," enabling scalable 1-to-N deployment as policies improve (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000062).

HITL-TAMP (Mandlekar et al. 2023, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2310.16014) used a TAMP-gated control mechanism that "enables the human teleoperator to manage a fleet of robots, maximizing data collection efficiency," gathering more than 3× the demonstrations given the same time budget compared to conventional teleoperation.

### Network Latency Effects

Bray et al. (2024, DOI: 10.3390/fi16120457) measured average round-trip latencies of 6.6 ms locally, 58.4 ms over Wi-Fi, 115.4 ms over cellular, and 240.7 ms over a transatlantic VPN; at 240 ms, "the robot moves only slightly more than four times per second, making control more challenging, although object-grasping tasks remain feasible" (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043).

Cundar et al. (2023, DOI: 10.3390/s23208438) quantified the relationship for a 4-DOF teleultrasound robot: a WLAN configuration produced approximately 300 ms average delay and a maximum displacement error of 7.8 mm, while a VLAN configuration reduced average delay by 40% and maximum displacement error by 70% (pqac-00000041).

Rakita et al. (2020, DOI: 10.1145/3319502.3374838) distinguished onset latency from robot slowness in mimicry-control teleoperation, finding that "users can quickly develop strategies to adapt to slowness delays but not onset latency delays" (pqac-00000040).

Louca et al. (2024, DOI: 10.1145/3651993) found that "increased latency reduced performance in all metrics recorded" for robot arm teleoperation with delays up to 2.6 seconds, and that operators adopted a "move-and-wait" strategy that substantially increased task completion time (pqac-00000039).

**For the Vertical Cloud Lab's 34 ms median command latency**: this falls well within the low-latency regime (<60 ms) where Bray et al. found stable, reliable control. The primary risk is jitter and outlier latencies rather than the median value itself.

## (4) Intervention Logs as Training Data for Laboratory Arms

**No published evidence was found** of anyone treating the intervention log of a scripted or fiducial-guided laboratory arm as training data for a learned recovery or correction policy. Similarly, **no published comparison** of scripted-plus-fixtures, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over a long campaign was identified.

The closest analogue is RaC's approach of collecting recovery and correction segments during deployment and retraining iteratively (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047), but this was demonstrated on manipulation tasks (shirt hanging, lid sealing, takeout packing), not laboratory protocols. The LabRobFail benchmark (preprint, Wang et al. 2026, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2607.23704) provides a simulation-based failure taxonomy and correction-instruction generation for chemical laboratory operations, with over 20,000 labeled trajectories across 70+ task scenarios (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000038), but it does not report using real intervention logs from a deployed lab arm for policy training.

**This is an open research area** that the Vertical Cloud Lab would be well-positioned to pioneer: treating each human intervention during scripted operation as both a reliability data point and a training example for a learned recovery policy.

## (5) Statistical Methods for Intervention Rate Estimation

### Rate Estimation

Intervention counts per fixed number of operations are naturally modeled as count data. The Poisson distribution is the starting point, with the rate parameter λ giving interventions per operation. The negative-binomial model accommodates overdispersion (variance exceeding the mean), which is common in reliability data. Pradhan (2023) used "negative-binomial modeling" alongside "survival analysis, recurrent-event modeling" and reported failure rates as incidence rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals for industrial asset reliability (pqac-00000000). Jovan et al. (2022, DOI: 10.1007/s10514-022-10070-9) used a partially observable Poisson process to model count data from a 69-day mobile robot deployment, with negative-binomial extensions for overdispersed observations and Bayesian posterior credible intervals for rate estimation (pqac-00000000).

### Time-to-Event Models

Survival analysis (Cox proportional hazards, Weibull models) is appropriate for modeling time or operations to the next intervention. Recurrent-event models (Andersen-Gill, frailty models) handle the fact that the same robot experiences multiple interventions.

### Learning Curves and Change-Point Detection

When the controller is being improved, the intervention rate is expected to decrease over time. This creates a non-stationary process. Standard approaches include:
- **Piecewise-constant Poisson models** with change points at policy updates
- **Bayesian online change-point detection** (Adams and MacKay 2007) to detect when intervention rates shift
- **Log-linear models** of rate versus cumulative operations (reliability growth models, e.g., Crow-AMSAA)

### Confidence Sequences for Sequential Monitoring

Confidence sequences (Howard et al. 2021, *Annals of Statistics*) provide time-uniform confidence intervals that remain valid under continuous monitoring, avoiding the multiple-testing problems of repeated hypothesis testing. These are directly applicable to sequential monitoring of intervention rates during a campaign. **No published robotics paper was found that applies confidence sequences to intervention-rate monitoring.**

### Sample Size

For a Poisson rate with no covariates, detecting a halving of the intervention rate (from λ₁ to λ₁/2) with 80% power and α = 0.05 requires approximately 2×(z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)²/ln(2)² ≈ 65 events per condition. For 300 operations per condition, the campaign is well powered to detect moderate rate differences provided the baseline rate is ≥ 0.2 interventions per operation. For rare events (<5% intervention rate), negative-binomial or exact Poisson methods are needed, and 300 operations may yield only ~15 events, requiring exact confidence intervals.

### Pre-Registration with an Adaptive Controller

**This is an identified gap in the literature.** No published work combines pre-registration with a deliberately improved controller during the campaign. The recommended approach draws from adaptive clinical trial methodology:

1. **Pre-specify the analysis plan** including: (a) the primary outcome (mean operations between interventions), (b) the secondary outcome (intervention rate per operation), (c) the failure taxonomy (LabRobFail categories), (d) planned policy update points, and (e) the statistical model (piecewise negative-binomial with change points at each policy update).
2. **Use a blocked design**: within each block (before each policy update), the controller is fixed, enabling valid within-block rate estimation.
3. **Apply confidence sequences** for the cumulative rate, allowing continuous monitoring without inflating the type I error rate.
4. **Report both the within-block rates and the overall trajectory**, treating policy updates as known covariates rather than nuisance variation.
5. **Register the protocol** (e.g., on OSF or as a Registered Report) specifying the minimum sample size per block, the decision rule for policy updates, and the analysis pipeline before data collection begins.

The PREP-eval framework (Carro et al. 2026) provides a general pre-registration and reporting protocol for AI evaluations that could be adapted to this setting, though it does not specifically address robotics or adaptive controllers.

## Summary of Evidence Gaps

Three significant gaps were identified:

1. **No published HIL/interactive learning work on truly low-cost arms** (SO-100/SO-101, Koch, PiPER, or sub-$3k systems). All published systems use research-grade arms ($10k+).
2. **No published work treats intervention logs from scripted/fiducial-guided laboratory arms as training data** for learned recovery policies, nor compares scripted, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over extended campaigns.
3. **No published robotics paper combines confidence sequences, change-point detection, and pre-registration** for a reliability campaign with a deliberately improved controller. The statistical components exist individually in reliability engineering and clinical trial methodology but have not been assembled for this use case.

# Human Intervention Metrics, Interactive Learning, Remote Supervision, and Statistical Design for a Laboratory Robot Reliability Campaign

## (1) Intervention Definitions and Reporting Outside Chemistry

### Autonomous-Driving Disengagements

The most mature reporting framework for human interventions is the California DMV's Autonomous Vehicle Tester Program. Under California Code of Regulations §227.38, a disengagement is defined as "deactivation of autonomous mode after an autonomous-technology failure is detected or when safe operation requires the test driver to take immediate manual control" (pqac-00000002). Manufacturers must file monthly disengagement reports (form OL 311R) by the tenth day of each month, recording VIN, software version, GPS coordinates, initiator, cause categories, and post-event actions; separate collision reports (form OL 316) are required within ten days, and hard-braking events above 0.5 g are reported monthly (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005). 

Disengagements are classified by initiator—system-initiated (automated), driver-initiated (manual), or planned for testing—and by cause categories including perception/localization/planning errors, environmental factors, and interactions with other road users (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). The primary performance metric is the disengagement-to-mileage ratio (disengagements per mile or its reciprocal, miles between interventions), though the DMV does not prescribe a standard calculation formula (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Banerjee et al. (2018) analyzed 1,116,605 autonomous miles, 5,328 disengagements, and 42 accidents from 144 vehicles across 12 manufacturers (pqac-00000001). Paz et al. (2020) emphasized that raw disengagement counts are insufficient without normalization by distance, operating time, testing location, and number of vehicles (pqac-00000000). Skokan and Mareček (2025) warned that "manufacturers' reporting thresholds and safety drivers' intervention decisions vary substantially," so reported rates reflect "technical performance, operating conditions, reporting practices, and individual driver risk tolerance" rather than a fully standardized safety measure (pqac-00000006).

### Fleet Learning: Return on Human Effort (ROHE)

For robot fleets, Hoque et al. (2022) formalized Interactive Fleet Learning (IFL) and introduced ROHE as "the expected cumulative fleet reward divided by total human assistance time, with normalization by the numbers of robots and supervisors and an added one in the denominator for the zero-assistance case" (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011). Fleet-DAgger evaluated allocation with 100 simulated robots and a physical experiment with four ABB YuMi arms and two remote human supervisors, achieving up to 8.8× higher ROHE than baselines (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000052).

### Transferability to a Laboratory Arm

Several of these definitions transfer directly:

- **Disengagement-style counting**: Any moment a remote operator takes control or the system is paused maps to an AV disengagement. The LabRobFail taxonomy (preprint, Wang et al. 2026) provides a lab-specific coding scheme with five major categories—Perception Failure (PF), Grasping Failure (GF), Motion Failure (MF), Logic Failure (LF), and Safety Failure (SF)—and 11 fine-grained failure types, plus four severity levels L1–L4 (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037).
- **Operations between interventions** (analogous to miles between disengagements) is the natural lab-arm metric: mean interventions between failures (MIBF) or its reciprocal.
- **ROHE** can be adapted: cumulative successful transfers divided by total human-supervision time.
- **Intervention sample ratio**: Sirius defined this as "the fraction of timesteps completed by humans relative to total trajectory timesteps," reporting a mean of 0.32 with SD 0.11 (pqac-00000020).

**No published standard or reporting checklist** exists specifically for laboratory robot arms. The LabRobFail benchmark is the closest laboratory-specific framework but is simulation-based and was published as a preprint (pqac-00000032).

## (2) Human-in-the-Loop Learning on Real Robots

The following table summarizes the major systems and their reported metrics:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### Key Results by System

**HG-DAgger** (Kelly et al. 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8793698) introduced human-gated interactive imitation learning where "the human expert determines when to intervene and take control of the robot." When reimplemented as a baseline in HIL-SERL, HG-DAgger averaged only 49.7% success with no consistent decline in intervention rate (pqac-00000025).

**Sirius** (Liu et al. 2024, DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273901) introduced intervention-weighted behavioral cloning on a Franka Emika Panda. The weighting scheme "up-weights interventions and down-weights pre-interventions" using approximated human trust (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000019). Across deployment data, the mean intervention sample ratio was 0.32 (SD 0.11), with an average of 2.80 interventions per trajectory and 15.28 timesteps per intervention (pqac-00000020). Policy success rates ranged from 44.8% to 72.7% across individual operators, with an overall 27% improvement over baselines on real hardware (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000017).

**HIL-SERL** (Luo et al. 2025, DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.ads5033, *Science Robotics*) achieved 100% success on all 13 evaluated tasks within 1–2.5 hours of real-world training, with the intervention rate declining to 0% as policies converged, while HG-DAgger baselines averaged 49.7% success (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029). Training began with approximately 20–30 human demonstrations (pqac-00000027). In a separate evaluation (Lin et al. 2026), HIL-SERL showed human intervention rates of 39–77% across five manipulation tasks before convergence (pqac-00000031).

**RaC** (Hu et al. 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2509.07953, *IEEE Transactions on Robotics*) uses two xArm-7 manipulators and explicitly teaches recovery-then-correction behavior. It achieved 78.3% full-task success on shirt hanging with approximately 5 hours of data versus 75% for ALOHA Unleashed with approximately 89 hours (pqac-00000049). In a head-to-head comparison, RaC achieved 61/100 successful trials versus 22/100 for HG-DAgger (pqac-00000051). Recovery-to-correction frame ratios were maintained at approximately 1:1 to 1:2, and total intervention frames decreased across rounds (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051).

### Low-Cost Arms

**No published HIL/interactive-learning work was found on SO-100, SO-101, Koch, or PiPER arms.** The closest low-cost platform is the xArm-7 used in RaC (pqac-00000046). The ALOHA system uses ViperX arms for bimanual teleoperation but its published work focuses on demonstration collection rather than online interactive learning with intervention-rate tracking. This represents a significant gap: all published HIL-RL and interactive IL systems with reported intervention metrics have used research-grade arms (Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, UR5, xArm-7).

### Laboratory or SDL Tasks

**No published evidence was found** of HIL interactive learning applied to self-driving laboratory tasks or chemical/materials manipulation. This is an open area.

## (3) Remote Supervision and Shared Autonomy

### One-to-Many Supervision

Fleet-DAgger formalized the problem of allocating M remote supervisors to N >> M robots, with physical experiments involving four ABB YuMi arms and two remote humans teleoperating over the Internet (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054). Hoque's dissertation describes remote fleet supervision using a cloud robotics platform supporting "real-time operation with robots, compute nodes, and teleoperators distributed globally" and reports a 10 Hz control loop over the Internet (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055). However, Fleet-DAgger's formal model "assumes that supervisors have perfect situational awareness, can switch between robots without any switching latency, and operate in synchronous timesteps without network latency or communication issues" and identifies removing these assumptions as future work (pqac-00000059).

Genie Centurion (GCENT, preprint, Wang et al. 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2505.18793) demonstrated one-human-to-two-robot supervision in a sandwich-assembly task. As model success rose from 40% to 80%, the intervention rate fell from 47% to 27%, while normalized collection efficiency rose from 1.86 to 1.92 (pqac-00000061). GCENT's Task Sentinel autonomously detects incomplete steps and "requests human intervention when needed," enabling scalable 1-to-N deployment as policies improve (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000062).

HITL-TAMP (Mandlekar et al. 2023, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2310.16014) used a TAMP-gated control mechanism that "enables the human teleoperator to manage a fleet of robots, maximizing data collection efficiency," gathering more than 3× the demonstrations given the same time budget compared to conventional teleoperation.

### Network Latency Effects

Bray et al. (2024, DOI: 10.3390/fi16120457) measured average round-trip latencies of 6.6 ms locally, 58.4 ms over Wi-Fi, 115.4 ms over cellular, and 240.7 ms over a transatlantic VPN; at 240 ms, "the robot moves only slightly more than four times per second, making control more challenging, although object-grasping tasks remain feasible" (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043).

Cundar et al. (2023, DOI: 10.3390/s23208438) quantified the relationship for a 4-DOF teleultrasound robot: a WLAN configuration produced approximately 300 ms average delay and a maximum displacement error of 7.8 mm, while a VLAN configuration reduced average delay by 40% and maximum displacement error by 70% (pqac-00000041).

Rakita et al. (2020, DOI: 10.1145/3319502.3374838) distinguished onset latency from robot slowness in mimicry-control teleoperation, finding that "users can quickly develop strategies to adapt to slowness delays but not onset latency delays" (pqac-00000040).

Louca et al. (2024, DOI: 10.1145/3651993) found that "increased latency reduced performance in all metrics recorded" for robot arm teleoperation with delays up to 2.6 seconds, and that operators adopted a "move-and-wait" strategy that substantially increased task completion time (pqac-00000039).

**For the Vertical Cloud Lab's 34 ms median command latency**: this falls well within the low-latency regime (<60 ms) where Bray et al. found stable, reliable control. The primary risk is jitter and outlier latencies rather than the median value itself.

## (4) Intervention Logs as Training Data for Laboratory Arms

**No published evidence was found** of anyone treating the intervention log of a scripted or fiducial-guided laboratory arm as training data for a learned recovery or correction policy. Similarly, **no published comparison** of scripted-plus-fixtures, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over a long campaign was identified.

The closest analogue is RaC's approach of collecting recovery and correction segments during deployment and retraining iteratively (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047), but this was demonstrated on manipulation tasks (shirt hanging, lid sealing, takeout packing), not laboratory protocols. The LabRobFail benchmark (preprint, Wang et al. 2026, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2607.23704) provides a simulation-based failure taxonomy and correction-instruction generation for chemical laboratory operations, with over 20,000 labeled trajectories across 70+ task scenarios (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000038), but it does not report using real intervention logs from a deployed lab arm for policy training.

**This is an open research area** that the Vertical Cloud Lab would be well-positioned to pioneer: treating each human intervention during scripted operation as both a reliability data point and a training example for a learned recovery policy.

## (5) Statistical Methods for Intervention Rate Estimation

### Rate Estimation

Intervention counts per fixed number of operations are naturally modeled as count data. The Poisson distribution is the starting point, with the rate parameter λ giving interventions per operation. The negative-binomial model accommodates overdispersion (variance exceeding the mean), which is common in reliability data. Pradhan (2023) used "negative-binomial modeling" alongside "survival analysis, recurrent-event modeling" and reported failure rates as incidence rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals for industrial asset reliability (pqac-00000000). Jovan et al. (2022, DOI: 10.1007/s10514-022-10070-9) used a partially observable Poisson process to model count data from a 69-day mobile robot deployment, with negative-binomial extensions for overdispersed observations and Bayesian posterior credible intervals for rate estimation (pqac-00000000).

### Time-to-Event Models

Survival analysis (Cox proportional hazards, Weibull models) is appropriate for modeling time or operations to the next intervention. Recurrent-event models (Andersen-Gill, frailty models) handle the fact that the same robot experiences multiple interventions.

### Learning Curves and Change-Point Detection

When the controller is being improved, the intervention rate is expected to decrease over time. This creates a non-stationary process. Standard approaches include:
- **Piecewise-constant Poisson models** with change points at policy updates
- **Bayesian online change-point detection** (Adams and MacKay 2007) to detect when intervention rates shift
- **Log-linear models** of rate versus cumulative operations (reliability growth models, e.g., Crow-AMSAA)

### Confidence Sequences for Sequential Monitoring

Confidence sequences (Howard et al. 2021, *Annals of Statistics*) provide time-uniform confidence intervals that remain valid under continuous monitoring, avoiding the multiple-testing problems of repeated hypothesis testing. These are directly applicable to sequential monitoring of intervention rates during a campaign. **No published robotics paper was found that applies confidence sequences to intervention-rate monitoring.**

### Sample Size

For a Poisson rate with no covariates, detecting a halving of the intervention rate (from λ₁ to λ₁/2) with 80% power and α = 0.05 requires approximately 2×(z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)²/ln(2)² ≈ 65 events per condition. For 300 operations per condition, the campaign is well powered to detect moderate rate differences provided the baseline rate is ≥ 0.2 interventions per operation. For rare events (<5% intervention rate), negative-binomial or exact Poisson methods are needed, and 300 operations may yield only ~15 events, requiring exact confidence intervals.

### Pre-Registration with an Adaptive Controller

**This is an identified gap in the literature.** No published work combines pre-registration with a deliberately improved controller during the campaign. The recommended approach draws from adaptive clinical trial methodology:

1. **Pre-specify the analysis plan** including: (a) the primary outcome (mean operations between interventions), (b) the secondary outcome (intervention rate per operation), (c) the failure taxonomy (LabRobFail categories), (d) planned policy update points, and (e) the statistical model (piecewise negative-binomial with change points at each policy update).
2. **Use a blocked design**: within each block (before each policy update), the controller is fixed, enabling valid within-block rate estimation.
3. **Apply confidence sequences** for the cumulative rate, allowing continuous monitoring without inflating the type I error rate.
4. **Report both the within-block rates and the overall trajectory**, treating policy updates as known covariates rather than nuisance variation.
5. **Register the protocol** (e.g., on OSF or as a Registered Report) specifying the minimum sample size per block, the decision rule for policy updates, and the analysis pipeline before data collection begins.

The PREP-eval framework (Carro et al. 2026) provides a general pre-registration and reporting protocol for AI evaluations that could be adapted to this setting, though it does not specifically address robotics or adaptive controllers.

## Summary of Evidence Gaps

Three significant gaps were identified:

1. **No published HIL/interactive learning work on truly low-cost arms** (SO-100/SO-101, Koch, PiPER, or sub-$3k systems). All published systems use research-grade arms ($10k+).
2. **No published work treats intervention logs from scripted/fiducial-guided laboratory arms as training data** for learned recovery policies, nor compares scripted, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over extended campaigns.
3. **No published robotics paper combines confidence sequences, change-point detection, and pre-registration** for a reliability campaign with a deliberately improved controller. The statistical components exist individually in reliability engineering and clinical trial methodology but have not been assembled for this use case.

We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, no certified safety functions), an SO-101 leader arm that teleoperates the PiPER (34 ms median command latency on the lab network), Raspberry Pi 5 wrist and fixed cameras, AprilTags, 3D-printed fixtures, and remote users who start runs from GitHub comments that launch AI-agent sessions, so the people supervising a run are often not in the room. Question.
(1) Outside chemistry, how have deployed robot systems defined, counted and reported human interventions: autonomous-driving disengagements, warehouse and mobile-manipulation fleets, household and service robots, surgical and field robots, and interactive fleet learning (for example Fleet-DAgger and its "return on human effort")? Which definitions (intervention types, severity levels, time to recover, operations or hours between interventions, human effort per robot-hour) would transfer to a laboratory arm, and which standards or proposed reporting checklists exist?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints. For each claim give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

# Human Intervention Metrics, Interactive Learning, Remote Supervision, and Statistical Design for a Laboratory Robot Reliability Campaign

## (1) Intervention Definitions and Reporting Outside Chemistry

### Autonomous-Driving Disengagements

The most mature reporting framework for human interventions is the California DMV's Autonomous Vehicle Tester Program. Under California Code of Regulations §227.38, a disengagement is defined as "deactivation of autonomous mode after an autonomous-technology failure is detected or when safe operation requires the test driver to take immediate manual control" (skokan2025coulddisengagementreports pages 2-4). Manufacturers must file monthly disengagement reports (form OL 311R) by the tenth day of each month, recording VIN, software version, GPS coordinates, initiator, cause categories, and post-event actions; separate collision reports (form OL 316) are required within ten days, and hard-braking events above 0.5 g are reported monthly (skokan2025coulddisengagementreports pages 2-4, kohanpour2025trendsinautonomous pages 4-7). 

Disengagements are classified by initiator—system-initiated (automated), driver-initiated (manual), or planned for testing—and by cause categories including perception/localization/planning errors, environmental factors, and interactions with other road users (kohanpour2025trendsinautonomous pages 1-2, kohanpour2025trendsinautonomous pages 2-4). The primary performance metric is the disengagement-to-mileage ratio (disengagements per mile or its reciprocal, miles between interventions), though the DMV does not prescribe a standard calculation formula (paz2020autonomousvehiclebenchmarking pages 1-2, banerjee2018handsoffthe pages 1-2). Banerjee et al. (2018) analyzed 1,116,605 autonomous miles, 5,328 disengagements, and 42 accidents from 144 vehicles across 12 manufacturers (banerjee2018handsoffthe pages 1-2). Paz et al. (2020) emphasized that raw disengagement counts are insufficient without normalization by distance, operating time, testing location, and number of vehicles (paz2020autonomousvehiclebenchmarking pages 1-2). Skokan and Mareček (2025) warned that "manufacturers' reporting thresholds and safety drivers' intervention decisions vary substantially," so reported rates reflect "technical performance, operating conditions, reporting practices, and individual driver risk tolerance" rather than a fully standardized safety measure (skokan2025coulddisengagementreports pages 16-18).

### Fleet Learning: Return on Human Effort (ROHE)

For robot fleets, Hoque et al. (2022) formalized Interactive Fleet Learning (IFL) and introduced ROHE as "the expected cumulative fleet reward divided by total human assistance time, with normalization by the numbers of robots and supervisors and an added one in the denominator for the zero-assistance case" (hoque2024scalablelifelongimitationa pages 64-66, hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 2-4). Fleet-DAgger evaluated allocation with 100 simulated robots and a physical experiment with four ABB YuMi arms and two remote human supervisors, achieving up to 8.8× higher ROHE than baselines (hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 1-2).

### Transferability to a Laboratory Arm

Several of these definitions transfer directly:

- **Disengagement-style counting**: Any moment a remote operator takes control or the system is paused maps to an AV disengagement. The LabRobFail taxonomy (preprint, Wang et al. 2026) provides a lab-specific coding scheme with five major categories—Perception Failure (PF), Grasping Failure (GF), Motion Failure (MF), Logic Failure (LF), and Safety Failure (SF)—and 11 fine-grained failure types, plus four severity levels L1–L4 (wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 1-2, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 2-3, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 4-5, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 8-10).
- **Operations between interventions** (analogous to miles between disengagements) is the natural lab-arm metric: mean interventions between failures (MIBF) or its reciprocal.
- **ROHE** can be adapted: cumulative successful transfers divided by total human-supervision time.
- **Intervention sample ratio**: Sirius defined this as "the fraction of timesteps completed by humans relative to total trajectory timesteps," reporting a mean of 0.32 with SD 0.11 (liu2024robotlearningon pages 13-14).

**No published standard or reporting checklist** exists specifically for laboratory robot arms. The LabRobFail benchmark is the closest laboratory-specific framework but is simulation-based and was published as a preprint (wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 1-2).

## (2) Human-in-the-Loop Learning on Real Robots

The following table summarizes the major systems and their reported metrics:

### Key Results by System

**HG-DAgger** (Kelly et al. 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8793698) introduced human-gated interactive imitation learning where "the human expert determines when to intervene and take control of the robot." **Sirius** (Liu et al. 2024, DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273901) introduced intervention-weighted behavioral cloning on a Franka Emika Panda. The weighting scheme "up-weights interventions and down-weights pre-interventions" using approximated human trust (liu2024robotlearningon pages 1-2, liu2024robotlearningon pages 7-8). Across deployment data, the mean intervention sample ratio was 0.32 (SD 0.11), with an average of 2.80 interventions per trajectory and 15.28 timesteps per intervention (liu2024robotlearningon pages 13-14). Policy success rates ranged from 44.8% to 72.7% across individual operators, with an overall 27% improvement over baselines on real hardware (liu2024robotlearningon pages 11-13, liu2024robotlearningon pages 1-2).

**HIL-SERL** (Luo et al. 2025, DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.ads5033, *Science Robotics*) achieved 100% success on all 13 evaluated tasks within 1–2.5 hours of real-world training, with the intervention rate declining to 0% as policies converged, while HG-DAgger baselines averaged 49.7% success (luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 14-15, luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 12-14, luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 1-3). Training began with approximately 20–30 human demonstrations (luo2025preciseanddexterous pages 8-9). In a separate evaluation (Lin et al. 2026), HIL-SERL showed human intervention rates of 39–77% across five manipulation tasks before convergence (lin2026uniintervene++anadaptive pages 4-5).

**RaC** (Hu et al. 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2509.07953, *IEEE Transactions on Robotics*) uses two xArm-7 manipulators and explicitly teaches recovery-then-correction behavior. It achieved 78.3% full-task success on shirt hanging with approximately 5 hours of data versus 75% for ALOHA Unleashed with approximately 89 hours (hu2026racrobotlearning pages 12-13). In a head-to-head comparison, RaC achieved 61/100 successful trials versus 22/100 for HG-DAgger (hu2026racrobotlearning pages 13-15). Recovery-to-correction frame ratios were maintained at approximately 1:1 to 1:2, and total intervention frames decreased across rounds (hu2026racrobotlearning pages 6-8, hu2026racrobotlearning pages 13-15).

### Low-Cost Arms

**No published HIL/interactive-learning work was found on SO-100, SO-101, Koch, or PiPER arms.** The closest low-cost platform is the xArm-7 used in RaC (hu2026racrobotlearning pages 4-6). The ALOHA system uses ViperX arms for bimanual teleoperation but its published work focuses on demonstration collection rather than online interactive learning with intervention-rate tracking. This represents a significant gap: all published HIL-RL and interactive IL systems with reported intervention metrics have used research-grade arms (Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, UR5, xArm-7).

### Laboratory or SDL Tasks

**No published evidence was found** of HIL interactive learning applied to self-driving laboratory tasks or chemical/materials manipulation. This is an open area.

## (3) Remote Supervision and Shared Autonomy

### One-to-Many Supervision

Fleet-DAgger formalized the problem of allocating M remote supervisors to N >> M robots, with physical experiments involving four ABB YuMi arms and two remote humans teleoperating over the Internet (hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 1-2, hoque2024scalablelifelongimitationa pages 61-64). Hoque's dissertation describes remote fleet supervision using a cloud robotics platform supporting "real-time operation with robots, compute nodes, and teleoperators distributed globally" and reports a 10 Hz control loop over the Internet (hoque2024scalablelifelongimitationa pages 12-15, hoque2024scalablelifelongimitation pages 12-15). However, Fleet-DAgger's formal model "assumes that supervisors have perfect situational awareness, can switch between robots without any switching latency, and operate in synchronous timesteps without network latency or communication issues" and identifies removing these assumptions as future work (hoque2022fleetdaggerinteractiverobot pages 8-10).

Genie Centurion (GCENT, preprint, Wang et al. 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2505.18793) demonstrated one-human-to-two-robot supervision in a sandwich-assembly task. As model success rose from 40% to 80%, the intervention rate fell from 47% to 27%, while normalized collection efficiency rose from 1.86 to 1.92 (wang2025geniecenturionaccelerating pages 7-9). GCENT's Task Sentinel autonomously detects incomplete steps and "requests human intervention when needed," enabling scalable 1-to-N deployment as policies improve (wang2025geniecenturionaccelerating pages 5-7, wang2025geniecenturionaccelerating pages 1-3).

HITL-TAMP (Mandlekar et al. 2023, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2310.16014) used a TAMP-gated control mechanism that "enables the human teleoperator to manage a fleet of robots, maximizing data collection efficiency," gathering more than 3× the demonstrations given the same time budget compared to conventional teleoperation.

### Network Latency Effects

Bray et al. (2024, DOI: 10.3390/fi16120457) measured average round-trip latencies of 6.6 ms locally, 58.4 ms over Wi-Fi, 115.4 ms over cellular, and 240.7 ms over a transatlantic VPN; at 240 ms, "the robot moves only slightly more than four times per second, making control more challenging, although object-grasping tasks remain feasible" (bray2024alatencycomposition pages 1-2, bray2024alatencycomposition pages 16-19).

Cundar et al. (2023, DOI: 10.3390/s23208438) quantified the relationship for a 4-DOF teleultrasound robot: a WLAN configuration produced approximately 300 ms average delay and a maximum displacement error of 7.8 mm, while a VLAN configuration reduced average delay by 40% and maximum displacement error by 70% (cundar2023quantifyingtheeffects pages 1-2).

Rakita et al. (2020, DOI: 10.1145/3319502.3374838) distinguished onset latency from robot slowness in mimicry-control teleoperation, finding that "users can quickly develop strategies to adapt to slowness delays but not onset latency delays" (rakita2020effectsofonset pages 1-2).

Louca et al. (2024, DOI: 10.1145/3651993) found that "increased latency reduced performance in all metrics recorded" for robot arm teleoperation with delays up to 2.6 seconds, and that operators adopted a "move-and-wait" strategy that substantially increased task completion time (louca2024impactofhaptic pages 1-3).

**For the Vertical Cloud Lab's 34 ms median command latency**: this falls well within the low-latency regime (<60 ms) where Bray et al. found stable, reliable control. The primary risk is jitter and outlier latencies rather than the median value itself.

## (4) Intervention Logs as Training Data for Laboratory Arms

**No published evidence was found** of anyone treating the intervention log of a scripted or fiducial-guided laboratory arm as training data for a learned recovery or correction policy. Similarly, **no published comparison** of scripted-plus-fixtures, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over a long campaign was identified.

The closest analogue is RaC's approach of collecting recovery and correction segments during deployment and retraining iteratively (hu2026racrobotlearning pages 4-6, hu2026racrobotlearning pages 2-4), but this was demonstrated on manipulation tasks (shirt hanging, lid sealing, takeout packing), not laboratory protocols. The LabRobFail benchmark (preprint, Wang et al. 2026, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2607.23704) provides a simulation-based failure taxonomy and correction-instruction generation for chemical laboratory operations, with over 20,000 labeled trajectories across 70+ task scenarios (wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 1-2, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 2-3, wang2026labrobfailabenchmark pages 3-4), but it does not report using real intervention logs from a deployed lab arm for policy training.

**This is an open research area** that the Vertical Cloud Lab would be well-positioned to pioneer: treating each human intervention during scripted operation as both a reliability data point and a training example for a learned recovery policy.

## (5) Statistical Methods for Intervention Rate Estimation

### Rate Estimation

Intervention counts per fixed number of operations are naturally modeled as count data. The Poisson distribution is the starting point, with the rate parameter λ giving interventions per operation. The negative-binomial model accommodates overdispersion (variance exceeding the mean), which is common in reliability data. Pradhan (2023) used "negative-binomial modeling" alongside "survival analysis, recurrent-event modeling" and reported failure rates as incidence rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals for industrial asset reliability (paz2020autonomousvehiclebenchmarking pages 1-2). Jovan et al. (2022, DOI: 10.1007/s10514-022-10070-9) used a partially observable Poisson process to model count data from a 69-day mobile robot deployment, with negative-binomial extensions for overdispersed observations and Bayesian posterior credible intervals for rate estimation (paz2020autonomousvehiclebenchmarking pages 1-2).

### Time-to-Event Models

Survival analysis (Cox proportional hazards, Weibull models) is appropriate for modeling time or operations to the next intervention. Recurrent-event models (Andersen-Gill, frailty models) handle the fact that the same robot experiences multiple interventions.

### Learning Curves and Change-Point Detection

When the controller is being improved, the intervention rate is expected to decrease over time. This creates a non-stationary process. Standard approaches include:
- **Piecewise-constant Poisson models** with change points at policy updates
- **Bayesian online change-point detection** (Adams and MacKay 2007) to detect when intervention rates shift
- **Log-linear models** of rate versus cumulative operations (reliability growth models, e.g., Crow-AMSAA)

### Confidence Sequences for Sequential Monitoring

Confidence sequences (Howard et al. 2021, *Annals of Statistics*) provide time-uniform confidence intervals that remain valid under continuous monitoring, avoiding the multiple-testing problems of repeated hypothesis testing. These are directly applicable to sequential monitoring of intervention rates during a campaign. **No published robotics paper was found that applies confidence sequences to intervention-rate monitoring.**

### Sample Size

For a Poisson rate with no covariates, detecting a halving of the intervention rate (from λ₁ to λ₁/2) with 80% power and α = 0.05 requires approximately 2×(z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)²/ln(2)² ≈ 65 events per condition. For 300 operations per condition, the campaign is well powered to detect moderate rate differences provided the baseline rate is ≥ 0.2 interventions per operation. For rare events (<5% intervention rate), negative-binomial or exact Poisson methods are needed, and 300 operations may yield only ~15 events, requiring exact confidence intervals.

### Pre-Registration with an Adaptive Controller

**This is an identified gap in the literature.** No published work combines pre-registration with a deliberately improved controller during the campaign. The recommended approach draws from adaptive clinical trial methodology:

1. **Pre-specify the analysis plan** including: (a) the primary outcome (mean operations between interventions), (b) the secondary outcome (intervention rate per operation), (c) the failure taxonomy (LabRobFail categories), (d) planned policy update points, and (e) the statistical model (piecewise negative-binomial with change points at each policy update).
2. **Use a blocked design**: within each block (before each policy update), the controller is fixed, enabling valid within-block rate estimation.
3. **Apply confidence sequences** for the cumulative rate, allowing continuous monitoring without inflating the type I error rate.
4. **Report both the within-block rates and the overall trajectory**, treating policy updates as known covariates rather than nuisance variation.
5. **Register the protocol** (e.g., on OSF or as a Registered Report) specifying the minimum sample size per block, the decision rule for policy updates, and the analysis pipeline before data collection begins.

The PREP-eval framework (Carro et al. 2026) provides a general pre-registration and reporting protocol for AI evaluations that could be adapted to this setting, though it does not specifically address robotics or adaptive controllers.

## Summary of Evidence Gaps

Three significant gaps were identified:

1. **No published HIL/interactive learning work on truly low-cost arms** (SO-100/SO-101, Koch, PiPER, or sub-$3k systems). All published systems use research-grade arms ($10k+).
2. **No published work treats intervention logs from scripted/fiducial-guided laboratory arms as training data** for learned recovery policies, nor compares scripted, learned, and hybrid controllers on intervention rate over extended campaigns.
3. **No published robotics paper combines confidence sequences, change-point detection, and pre-registration** for a reliability campaign with a deliberately improved controller. The statistical components exist individually in reliability engineering and clinical trial methodology but have not been assembled for this use case.

# Human Intervention Metrics, Interactive Learning, Remote Supervision, and Statistical Design for a Laboratory Robot Reliability Campaign

## (1) Intervention Definitions and Reporting Outside Chemistry

### Autonomous-Driving Disengagements

The most mature reporting framework for human interventions is the California DMV's Autonomous Vehicle Tester Program. Under California Code of Regulations §227.38, a disengagement is defined as "deactivation of autonomous mode after an autonomous-technology failure is detected or when safe operation requires the test driver to take immediate manual control" (pqac-00000002). Manufacturers must file monthly disengagement reports (form OL 311R) by the tenth day of each month, recording VIN, software version, GPS coordinates, initiator, cause categories, and post-event actions; separate collision reports (form OL 316) are required within ten days, and hard-braking events above 0.5 g are reported monthly (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005). 

Disengagements are classified by initiator—system-initiated (automated), driver-initiated (manual), or planned for testing—and by cause categories including perception/localization/planning errors, environmental factors, and interactions with other road users (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). The primary performance metric is the disengagement-to-mileage ratio (disengagements per mile or its reciprocal, miles between interventions), though the DMV does not prescribe a standard calculation formula (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Banerjee et al. (2018) analyzed 1,116,605 autonomous miles, 5,328 disengagements, and 42 accidents from 144 vehicles across 12 manufacturers (pqac-00000001). Paz et al. (2020) emphasized that raw disengagement counts are insufficient without normalization by distance, operating time, testing location, and number of vehicles (pqac-00000000). Skokan and Mareček (2025) warned that "manufacturers' reporting thresholds and safety drivers' intervention decisions vary substantially," so reported rates reflect "technical performance, operating conditions, reporting practices, and individual driver risk tolerance" rather than a fully standardized safety measure (pqac-00000006).

### Fleet Learning: Return on Human Effort (ROHE)

For robot fleets, Hoque et al. (2022) formalized Interactive Fleet Learning (IFL) and introduced ROHE as "the expected cumulative fleet reward divided by total human assistance time, with normalization by the numbers of robots and supervisors and an added one in the denominator for the zero-assistance case" (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011). Fleet-DAgger evaluated allocation with 100 simulated robots and a physical experiment with four ABB YuMi arms and two remote human supervisors, achieving up to 8.8× higher ROHE than baselines (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000052).

### Transferability to a Laboratory Arm

Several of these definitions transfer directly:

- **Disengagement-style counting**: Any moment a remote operator takes control or the system is paused maps to an AV disengagement. The LabRobFail taxonomy (preprint, Wang et al. 2026) provides a lab-specific coding scheme with five major categories—Perception Failure (PF), Grasping Failure (GF), Motion Failure (MF), Logic Failure (LF), and Safety Failure (SF)—and 11 fine-grained failure types, plus four severity levels L1–L4 (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037).
- **Operations between interventions** (analogous to miles between disengagements) is the natural lab-arm metric: mean interventions between failures (MIBF) or its reciprocal.
- **ROHE** can be adapted: cumulative successful transfers divided by total human-supervision time.
- **Intervention sample ratio**: Sirius defined this as "the fraction of timesteps completed by humans relative to total trajectory timesteps," reporting a mean of 0.32 with SD 0.11 (pqac-00000020).

**No published standard or reporting checklist** exists specifically for laboratory robot arms. The LabRobFail benchmark is the closest laboratory-specific framework but is simulation-based and was published as a preprint (pqac-00000032).
